newsitem.title: UK: Greenpeace challenges oil industry for new site.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace challenges oil industry for new site.

text.p: Environmental lobby group Greenpeace challenged Britain's oil industry on Tuesday by bidding for the rights to a major unexplored seabed site off the northern Scottish coast.
The British government said Greenpeace had bid against the world's leading oil companies for all 22,000 square miles of offshore acreage available in Britain's 17th oil licensing round.
Greenpeace said it hoped to block the multi-billion dollar aspirations of the international oil industry and turn the site into a marine wildlife sanctuary.
"Opening up pristine ocean for new oil development is madness fuelled by greed," said Greenpeace spokesman Matthew Spencer.
Greenpeace also said it had met British Petroleum to discuss concerns about the company's developments west of the Shetland islands.
British Petroleum said it had briefed Greenpeace on its intentions to start oil production at the Shetland Foinaven development, the first of a new generation of oilfields in the region.
"We did have a briefing on our operations west of Shetland with Greenpeace and we have written to them," said a company spokesman.
Greenpeace said rumours that it was planning to take direct action to sabotage British Petroleum's operations were started by the company.

"Greenpeace is surprised that BP has apparently started this rumour mill and expressed such concern when thus far all Greenpeace has done is discuss the issue with the oil industry," Greenpeace said in a statement.
Greenpeace campaign manager Sarah Burton said the group could not rule out the possibility of direct action.
"We haven't ruled it out because Greenpeace never discusses future action," she said.
In 1995, Greenpeace forced Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell to rethink its plans to ditch the Brent Spar platform at sea.
A high-profile campaign involved Greenpeace attempts to block the platform being towed to its dumping site and a boycott of Shell petrol stations in Europe.
Brent Spar has been moored in a Norwegian fjord since then. Alternative proposals for disposal are being assessed by an independent adviser.
British Petroleum is expecting to bring the Foinaven oilfield on stream in a matter of weeks after a fast-track development following government approval in 1994.
A second BP field, Schiehallion, is due onstream in mid-1998 and earlier this month the company announced a third discovery in the region, Suilven.
The British goverment said Greenpeace's application for the 17th round acreage was being assessed.
"We have received applications from Greenpeace and we are examining the documentation to see if they meet the legal requirements," a spokeswoman for the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) said.
She said 36 oil companies had applied for the 127 blocks on offer.
No decision had been made on when the awards would be made, she added.
Britain's offshore oil industry association said it was surprised by the Greenpeace application.

"Whatever Greenpeace might believe should be the case in the future, life today and the expectations of consumers with regard to living standards, comfort and mobility, depend on the availability of adequate resources of fossil fuels," UK Offshore Operators Association (UKOOA) director James May said.
UKOOA represents 34 oil companies licensed to explore for and produce oil and gas in British waters.
